metadata.name: id
metadata.displayName: id - Print user and group IDs

installation.note: id is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: The id command displays user and group identity information. It shows the current user's user ID (UID), group ID (GID), and all groups the user belongs to. It's essential for understanding permissions, debugging access issues, and checking user identity in scripts.
when_to_use: Check current user ID and group ID
See all groups a user belongs to

syntax.description: Display user and group IDs. If USER is specified, show that user's information. If omitted, show current user's information.

options.use_case: Get just the numeric user ID for scripts

options.description: Print only the primary group ID
options.use_case: Get just the primary group ID
Get all groups the user belongs to

options.description: Print names instead of numeric IDs
options.use_case: Get username instead of user ID

options.description: Print real ID instead of effective ID
options.use_case: Get real user ID (useful when running with sudo)

misconceptions.title: id shows file permissions
misconceptions.misconception: id shows what permissions you have on files
misconceptions.reality: id shows your user and group identity. Use ls -l to see file permissions, or test access with commands like test -r file.
misconceptions.tip: id shows who you are, not what you can access. Check file permissions separately.

misconceptions.title: Group membership grants immediate access
misconceptions.misconception: Adding a user to a group immediately grants access
misconceptions.reality: Users must log out and back in (or start new sessions) for new group memberships to take effect. Existing sessions don't see new groups.
misconceptions.tip: After adding a user to a group, they need to log out/in or start a new session for it to take effect

common_pitfalls.description: After being added to a group, id doesn't show the new group
common_pitfalls.solution: Log out and back in, or start a new shell session. Group changes require new session to take effect.

common_pitfalls.description: When using sudo, effective ID is root but real ID is your user
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -r flag to see real ID, or understand that sudo changes effective ID but not real ID

related_commands.relationship: User identity; whoami shows username, id shows detailed ID information
Group information; groups shows group names, id shows both IDs and names
related_commands.description: Print group names a user belongs to

related_commands.relationship: Privilege elevation; sudo changes effective ID, id shows both real and effective
related_commands.description: Execute a command as another user

best_practices: Use id -un to get username in scripts (more portable than $USER)
Use id -u to get numeric user ID for comparisons
Use id -G to check group memberships programmatically
Remember to log out/in after group membership changes
Use -r flag when checking identity with sudo to see real user
performance_tips: id is very fast - negligible performance impact
Use specific flags (-u, -g, -G) instead of parsing full output when you only need one value
id is more reliable than environment variables like $USER in scripts

additional_notes.user_id_zero: UID 0 is always the root/superuser account
additional_notes.group_membership: Users can belong to multiple groups - primary group and supplementary groups
additional_notes.real_vs_effective: Real ID is who you are, effective ID is who you're acting as (important with sudo/su)
additional_notes.scripting: id is more reliable than $USER or $UID environment variables, which can be changed
